name: BoringSSL
workload: Single-thread bssl speed versus openssl speed on RSA-2048 and ECDSA P-256 sign and verify operations per second, read off the two tool outputs by a forum poster in 2018.
claimed_speedup: Forum poster's reading: BoringSSL ECDSA P-256 sign ~9.55% faster and verify ~3.42% faster than OpenSSL 1.1.1-dev9 master; RSA-2048 sign ~1.6% faster but RSA-2048 verify ~4.55% slower. Percentages come from the search-result summaries of the thread; the raw speed tables were not read.
stars_or_usage: 2.3k stars on the GitHub mirror; the TLS library of Chromium and Android
tradeoffs: README says it is not intended for general use and gives no API or ABI stability guarantee; third parties are told not to depend on it. Not a drop-in OpenSSL replacement (features such as OCSP stapling are absent according to the same forum thread, snippet only).
caveats: Weak evidence, snippet only: the forum page was not opened (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND community.centminmod.com), so the percentages come from two WebSearch result summaries that agreed with each other. They are one user's reading of single-machine output; CPU, compiler, flags and BoringSSL commit are not stated, and the baseline is a 2018 OpenSSL 1.1.1 development build, now end-of-life. The result is mixed (RSA verify slower). Contradicting evidence that was opened: (1) the 2014 gist https://gist.github.com/tell/8135bd3ebb9aa67e1ff0 lists BoringSSL RSA-2048 sign at 882 ops/s against OpenSSL 1.0.1h at 1550 ops/s on the same Mac class of machine (separate runs, Core i7 3630QM), so BoringSSL slower; (2) https://github.com/soda4fries/ChaChaCha/blob/main/result.md (AMD EPYC 9655, Zen 5, cycles per byte, pinned core, perf_event_open) shows BoringSSL's stitched AVX2 ChaCha20-Poly1305 seal at 1.5204 c/B against OpenSSL assembly at 0.8409 c/B for 16 KiB records (BoringSSL about 1.8x slower, derived from page data). BoringSSL's own AES-GCM commit messages (VAES/VPCLMULQDQ commit) compare only against earlier BoringSSL code and a Cloudflare patch, not OpenSSL. boringssl.googlesource.com (the URL on the list) is not reachable from this environment; the GitHub mirror was used for repo facts.

name: Botan
workload: AES-128/GCM encryption of small buffers (16, 64, 256 bytes), botan speed output compared with openssl speed -evp output on one Skylake desktop; same thread shows OpenSSL ahead for buffers above 4 KiB.
claimed_speedup: Maintainer comment (Mar 31 2026), Botan 3.11.1 AES-128/GCM [clmul] encrypt: 16 B 107.584 MiB/s, 64 B 413.402 MiB/s, 256 B 1063.421 MiB/s; OpenSSL 3.6.0 AES-128-GCM: 73540.59k, 283567.77k, 942306.56k bytes/s at 16, 64, 256 B. That is about 1.5x at 16 B and 64 B and about 1.2x at 256 B for Botan (derived from page data, taking openssl speed k as 1000 bytes). Maintainer on Jul 21 2026: 'For small messages on my machine most recent Botan is faster than OpenSSL'; 'For large messages (> 4K) OpenSSL is still faster, at least on a Skylake processor'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 2026 runs. An Aug 28 2018 comment in the same thread on the same host used GCC 8.2 on Arch Linux with -march=skylake and 16 KiB buffers.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700K (Skylake) at 4 GHz, as named in the 2018 comments of the thread; the Mar 31 2026 comment says 'same machine as above comments'
tradeoffs: C++ library; hardware paths (AES-NI, CLMUL, AVX2, AVX-512) are chosen at run time, as the CPUID lines in the issue show. Per the same thread, large-message AES-GCM is slower than OpenSSL's assembly.
caveats: The winning claim is the maintainer's own, covers only small messages and is disputed in the same thread: on Jul 22 2026 the original poster ran Botan 3.12.0 (-march=znver4, AVX-512 CLMUL) against OpenSSL 4.0.1 on a Ryzen 9 7950X3D and got 54.84 cycles/byte (Botan) versus 20.31 (OpenSSL) at 16 B and 0.38 versus 0.25 at 16 KiB, concluding 'I cannot confirm that Botan is faster than OpenSSL, even for small messages'. The 2026 Skylake comment gives no compiler, flags or exact commands, and compares two different tools (botan speed, openssl speed) with different timing windows. Historical numbers in the same thread show OpenSSL 1.1.0e 12.2x faster than Botan 2.0.1 on AES-128/GCM (0.65 vs 7.94 cycles/byte) and 1.7 vs 7.34 on ChaCha20Poly1305, narrowed by Botan 2.8.0 to 2.2x and 2.4x. An independent harness, https://github.com/scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp (Botan 3.9.0 vs OpenSSL 3.6.0 on an unnamed Apple Silicon laptop, result.json), shows Botan slower than OpenSSL on SHA-256 (471 vs 2787 MB/s at 16 KiB), SHA-512, SHA3-256 and HMAC-SHA256, and only marginally ahead on 64-byte Poly1305 (393 vs 352 MB/s) and BLAKE2b (228 vs 214 MB/s). The thread page was read through WebFetch summaries; figures were cross-checked across two fetches.

name: Crypto++
baseline: libgcrypt (CAST5 in CBC mode), also Botan 1.10 (CAST_128)
workload: CAST-128 (CAST5) encryption and decryption of a 4096-byte buffer, 50000 rounds per implementation, timed with clock(), each round re-creating the cipher object and key schedule.
claimed_speedup: README sample output: Crypto++ CAST128 101.73 MB/s encrypt and 109.73 MB/s decrypt versus libgcrypt 75.70 and 76.00 MB/s (about 1.34x and 1.44x, derived from page data) and Botan 96.69 and 97.17 MB/s (about 1.05x and 1.13x, derived from page data); the Linux kernel AF_ALG path was faster than all three (135.10 and 315.98 MB/s).
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O2 -Wall -march=corei7-avx (from the Makefile); compiler and library versions not stated; Botan 1.10 headers
tradeoffs: Large C++ class library of cryptographic schemes under the Boost Software License 1.0 for the compilation (License.txt), individual files placed in the public domain, some CRYPTOGAMS code under a BSD-style licence; the API is filter and pipeline based.
caveats: Weak, old and third-party: a 2013 hobby repository (2 stars, 8 commits) with a sample output only, no CPU model, no library versions. The three C++/C implementations are not like for like: Botan is called as a bare encrypt_n block loop (no chaining mode) while Crypto++ and libgcrypt run CBC; Crypto++ goes through StringSource, StreamTransformationFilter and StringSink with heap allocation (the sample shows 412 MB of malloc traffic for encrypt) and every round repeats key setup and object creation. CAST-128 is a legacy cipher, so the result says little about AES or SHA performance. Current independent data points the other way: https://github.com/scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp (Crypto++ 8.9.0 vs OpenSSL 3.6.0, unnamed Apple Silicon laptop, result.json) has Crypto++ far behind OpenSSL, e.g. AES-128-GCM 54 vs 7880 MB/s and SHA-256 71 vs 2787 MB/s at 16 KiB, probably because ARM crypto instructions were not used; and the 2014 gist https://gist.github.com/aalness/577c7a6da1e669a07db9 has Crypto++ SHA-256 slower than OpenSSL (286 ms vs 162 ms for 300000 32-byte hashes; 19195 ms vs 17554.8 ms at 8192 bytes), though about 2x faster than libsecp256k1's own SHA-256. The Crypto++ repository itself publishes no cross-library comparison (its README only lists benchmarks as a feature).
